q: An auditor wants to obtain evidence that all goods shipped during the year were billed and recorded as sales. Which procedure best addresses this objective?
choices: Select recorded sales invoices and vouch them to shipping documents
Select shipping documents and trace them to sales invoices and the sales journal
Confirm year-end accounts receivable balances with customers
Recalculate the extensions and footings on a sample of sales invoices
exp: Starting from the shipping documents and tracing forward to recorded sales tests completeness, because it can reveal shipments that were never billed. Vouching recorded invoices back to shipping documents runs in the opposite direction and tests occurrence, not completeness.

q: An auditor is concerned that recorded sales include fictitious transactions. Which procedure provides the most direct evidence about this risk?
choices: Trace a sample of bills of lading to entries in the sales journal
Account for the numerical sequence of prenumbered shipping documents
Vouch a sample of sales journal entries to approved customer orders and shipping documents
Compare the gross margin percentage with the prior year
exp: Fictitious sales are an occurrence (overstatement) risk, so the auditor starts with recorded entries and vouches them back to evidence that a real order and shipment existed. Tracing bills of lading forward and accounting for document sequence test completeness, the opposite direction.

q: Which procedure is most effective in detecting sales recorded in the wrong period near year-end?
choices: Compare shipping dates on documents for several days before and after year-end with the dates the related sales were recorded
Send positive confirmations to customers with the largest balances
Review the aged trial balance for accounts more than 90 days past due
Test the approval of credit for a sample of sales orders throughout the year
exp: A sales cutoff test compares the shipment or transfer-of-control date with the recording date for transactions just before and after the period end. Confirmations mainly address existence of balances, and aging and credit tests address valuation.

q: A customer did not respond to a positive accounts receivable confirmation request, even after a second request. Which alternative procedure would generally provide the best evidence that the balance exists?
choices: Obtain a written representation from the client's credit manager about the balance
Recompute the balance using the client's accounts receivable subsidiary ledger
Send a negative confirmation request to the same customer
Examine cash received after year-end that is specifically identified with invoices in the balance
exp: Subsequent cash receipts matched to the specific invoices that made up the year-end balance provide strong external evidence that the receivable existed. Internal representations and recomputing the ledger rely on client records, and a negative request to a customer who ignored a positive request adds little evidence.

q: Under AU-C 505, negative confirmation requests may be used as the sole substantive procedure for receivables only when several conditions are met. Which of the following is one of those conditions?
choices: The population consists of a small number of large balances
The auditor expects a high rate of exceptions
The assessed risk of material misstatement is low and the auditor has obtained evidence about the operating effectiveness of relevant controls
The customers are not expected to read the requests carefully
exp: Negative confirmations provide less persuasive evidence, so they are appropriate alone only when risk is low and controls evidence supports that assessment, the population is a large number of small homogeneous balances, a very low exception rate is expected, and recipients are expected to give the requests consideration. A small number of large balances calls for positive requests.

q: AU-C 240 directs the auditor to presume a particular fraud risk unless it is rebutted. Which statement about that presumption is correct?
choices: The auditor presumes there is a fraud risk related to revenue recognition and must document the reasons if the presumption is overcome
The auditor presumes there is a fraud risk related to inventory and must count inventory at year-end
The auditor presumes revenue is fairly stated unless fraud risk factors are identified
The presumption applies only to public companies with revenue-based compensation plans
exp: AU-C 240 requires the auditor to presume a risk of material misstatement due to fraud in revenue recognition and, if the auditor concludes the presumption does not apply, to document the reasons. The presumption applies to all audits under GAAS, not only to public companies.

q: Client receivables at year-end are aged as follows, with estimated uncollectible rates: current $400,000 (1%), 31-60 days $100,000 (5%), 61-90 days $50,000 (20%), over 90 days $20,000 (50%). Before adjustment, the allowance has a $12,000 credit balance. What year-end allowance balance is supported by the aging?
exp: Required allowance = $4,000 + $5,000 + $10,000 + $10,000 = $29,000. The $17,000 figure is the adjustment needed ($29,000 − $12,000), which equals bad debt expense under the aging method, not the ending allowance balance.

q: Positive confirmation of accounts receivable provides the most reliable evidence about which assertion?
choices: Valuation, because customers report whether they intend to pay
Existence, because customers confirm that they owe the recorded amounts
Completeness, because customers report balances the client failed to record
Rights and obligations, because customers report whether receivables are pledged
exp: A positive confirmation is external evidence that the recorded receivable exists. A customer can acknowledge a debt and still be unable or unwilling to pay, so confirmations give limited evidence about valuation, and they rarely reveal unrecorded balances.

q: A client had net credit sales of $3,650,000 and year-end accounts receivable of $500,000. Last year, days sales outstanding were 36 days. Using a 365-day year and year-end receivables, what are current-year days sales outstanding, and what might the change indicate?
choices: 50 days; possible collectibility problems or fictitious sales
50 days; improved collection efficiency
36 days; no change requiring follow-up
7.3 days; receivables turning over faster than last year
exp: Average daily sales are $3,650,000 ÷ 365 = $10,000, so DSO = $500,000 ÷ $10,000 = 50 days. An increase from 36 to 50 days means receivables are collected more slowly, which can signal valuation problems or recorded sales that will never be collected; 7.3 is the turnover ratio, not days.

q: Which procedure is most likely to detect lapping of customer payments?
choices: Confirm the year-end bank balance with the bank
Compare the dates and customer details on deposited remittance advices with the dates and accounts credited in the receivables ledger
Review the aged trial balance for credit balances
Recalculate the allowance for doubtful accounts
exp: Lapping conceals a stolen payment by applying a later customer's payment to the earlier account, so the payer and date on remittances and deposit details will not agree with the postings. A bank confirmation would agree with deposits and would not reveal that payments were credited to the wrong customers.

q: Which segregation of duties is most important to reduce the risk that cash receipts from customers are stolen and the theft concealed?
choices: The credit manager should not approve sales returns
The shipping clerk should not prepare bills of lading
The sales manager should not set prices
The employee who handles customer remittances should not post to the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger
exp: An employee who has custody of receipts and can also record credits to customer accounts can steal cash and hide it, for example by lapping or writing off accounts. Separating custody from recordkeeping is the key control; the other separations address different risks.

q: Independent credit approval before goods are shipped primarily reduces the risk of misstatement related to which assertion for accounts receivable?
choices: Valuation
Existence
Completeness
Classification
exp: Credit approval limits sales to customers likely to pay, reducing the risk that receivables are uncollectible and overstated net of the allowance. It does not prevent fictitious sales or ensure all shipments are billed.

q: While reviewing January transactions, an auditor notes a large volume of credit memos for returns of goods shipped in the last week of December. What is the most likely implication?
choices: December revenue may be understated because returns were recorded in January
Year-end revenue and receivables may be overstated, possibly from channel stuffing
The allowance for doubtful accounts is overstated
The returns relate only to the next year and need no further work
exp: Heavy returns soon after year-end of goods shipped just before year-end suggest the goods were pushed to customers to inflate sales, overstating revenue and receivables and possibly requiring a refund liability. The auditor should investigate the terms and evaluate the estimate of returns.

q: An auditor sends accounts receivable confirmations electronically and receives responses by email. Which statement about these responses is consistent with AU-C 505?
choices: Electronic responses are never reliable and must be replaced with paper responses
Electronic responses are reliable only if they include a scanned signature
The auditor should consider the risk that the response was not from the intended party and may need to verify its source
The auditor may accept the responses without consideration because they were sent to addresses supplied by the client
exp: Responses received electronically involve risks to reliability, so the auditor considers whether they came from the proper source and were not intercepted or altered, and may verify the source if doubts exist. Electronic confirmations are acceptable; a client-supplied address is itself a reason for care, not a reason to skip it.

q: Management asks the auditor not to confirm the receivable from the client's largest customer, saying the customer is in a dispute and contact would harm the relationship. What should the auditor do first?
choices: Agree, and treat the request as a scope limitation requiring a disclaimer of opinion
Send the confirmation anyway because management cannot restrict the auditor's procedures
Inquire about management's reasons, seek evidence of their validity and reasonableness, and consider the effect on the fraud risk assessment
Agree, and rely on management's written representation about the balance
exp: AU-C 505 requires the auditor to inquire into management's reasons, seek evidence about their validity and reasonableness, evaluate implications for the assessment of risks including fraud, and perform alternative procedures. Only if the refusal is unreasonable or alternative evidence cannot be obtained does the auditor communicate with those charged with governance and consider the effect on the opinion.

q: A confirmation response states that the customer paid its balance on December 30. The client recorded the receipt on January 4. What is the auditor's most appropriate response?
choices: Treat the difference as a misstatement and project it to the population
Investigate the timing difference, including when the cash was received and deposited, to rule out lapping or misapplied payments
Ignore the difference because timing differences are never misstatements
Send a second confirmation to the customer asking it to change its response
exp: Timing differences are common and often not misstatements, but the auditor must investigate them, because a delay between payment and recording can also indicate lapping or misapplication of receipts. Treating it automatically as a misstatement, or ignoring it, both skip the required evaluation of the exception.

q: A client recorded sales of $2,000,000 and cost of sales of $1,320,000. Based on stable pricing, the auditor expected a gross margin of 40%. What difference between recorded and expected cost of sales should the auditor investigate?
exp: Expected cost of sales is $2,000,000 × (1 − 0.40) = $1,200,000, so recorded cost of sales exceeds expectation by $1,320,000 − $1,200,000 = $120,000. The $800,000 figure is the expected gross profit, not the difference to investigate.

q: An auditor suspects that sales personnel have granted customers unrecorded rights of return and extended payment terms. Which procedure is most responsive to this risk?
choices: Confirm with customers the terms of their sales agreements, including any side agreements, in addition to balances
Recompute the sales journal totals
Review the client's credit approval policies
Test the numerical sequence of sales invoices
exp: Side agreements are not visible in the client's records, so confirming contract terms directly with customers is the most direct way to identify them. Recomputing totals or testing invoice sequence would not reveal terms that were never documented by the client.

q: Under a $120,000 contract signed on July 1, a client sold equipment (standalone selling price $100,000) delivered that day, and a two-year service plan (standalone selling price $50,000) that starts the same day. The client recognized $120,000 of revenue in the year ended December 31. By how much is revenue overstated?
exp: Allocating by relative standalone selling price gives equipment $80,000 (100/150 × $120,000) and service $40,000; six of 24 months of service have passed, so service revenue is $10,000 and total revenue is $90,000. Overstatement = $120,000 − $90,000 = $30,000; $20,000 wrongly treats the full equipment SSP of $100,000 as earned.

q: Goods costing $30,000 were shipped FOB destination on December 30 and arrived at the customer on January 4. The client recorded a $50,000 sale and the related cost of sales on December 30. What is the effect on pretax income for the year ended December 31?
choices: Overstated by $50,000
Overstated by $30,000
Understated by $20,000
Overstated by $20,000
exp: Control passed on delivery in January, so both the $50,000 sale and the $30,000 cost of sales belong in the next year; pretax income is overstated by $50,000 − $30,000 = $20,000. The $50,000 answer ignores that cost of sales was also recorded early.

q: A client uses prenumbered shipping documents. An auditor accounts for the numerical sequence of those documents and investigates gaps. This control test primarily relates to which assertion for sales?
choices: Occurrence
Accuracy
Completeness
Cutoff
exp: Accounting for the sequence of prenumbered shipping documents helps ensure every shipment is captured and billed, which relates to completeness. Testing occurrence would require vouching recorded sales to supporting evidence.

q: A shipping clerk compares goods to be shipped with an approved sales order before releasing them. This control is primarily designed to prevent which of the following?
choices: Shipments to customers who have not placed or been approved for an order
Billing errors in unit prices
Failure to record shipped goods in the sales journal
Misclassification of sales between product lines
exp: Requiring an approved sales order before release prevents unauthorized shipments. It does not check invoice pricing, which is an accuracy control in billing, or ensure that shipments are recorded.

q: An auditor compares unit prices on a sample of sales invoices with the client's authorized price list. This procedure most directly tests which assertion?
choices: Completeness
Accuracy
Existence
Presentation
exp: Agreeing invoice prices to authorized prices tests whether transactions were recorded at the correct amounts, which is accuracy. It does not address whether the transactions occurred or whether all sales were recorded.

q: Which control is most effective in reducing the risk that customer checks received by mail are misappropriated?
choices: Monthly statements are mailed to customers by the receivables clerk
The controller approves write-offs of uncollectible accounts
Two mailroom employees open the mail together, restrictively endorse checks and prepare a list of remittances
Bank reconciliations are prepared by the cashier
exp: Establishing control at the point of receipt, with dual custody, immediate restrictive endorsement and an independent remittance list, prevents checks from being diverted. Statements mailed by the receivables clerk, or reconciliations prepared by the cashier, lack independence from the functions they check.

q: A client acts as an agent in arranging travel bookings but records the full ticket price as revenue and the airfare as cost of sales. What is the effect on the financial statements?
choices: Revenue and cost of sales are overstated, but gross profit is unchanged
Revenue is overstated and net income is overstated by the same amount
Revenue is understated because commissions should be grossed up
There is no misstatement because gross and net presentation are both acceptable
exp: An agent recognizes revenue for the net commission it earns, so gross presentation overstates both revenue and cost of sales by the airfare while leaving gross profit and net income unchanged. Gross versus net is determined by principal-versus-agent analysis under ASC 606, not by choice.

q: A client offers volume rebates, and management estimates the refund liability at year-end. Which approach is not one of the responses AU-C 540 identifies for testing this accounting estimate?
choices: Testing how management made the estimate, including its methods, assumptions and data
Developing an independent point estimate or range to evaluate management's estimate
Obtaining evidence from events occurring up to the date of the auditor's report
Accepting management's estimate because it is consistent with last year's method
exp: AU-C 540 responses include obtaining evidence from events through the report date, testing how management made the estimate, and developing an auditor's point estimate or range. Consistency with the prior-year method does not show the estimate is reasonable this year.

q: Which source of information would most likely alert the auditor that accounts receivable have been pledged as collateral?
choices: The aged trial balance of receivables
Sales invoices issued after year-end
Loan agreements, board minutes and the bank confirmation
Customer confirmation responses
exp: Pledging is a financing arrangement documented in loan agreements and board minutes and often reported on bank confirmations, and it must be disclosed. Customers usually do not know their balances are pledged, so their responses would not reveal it.

q: In testing journal entries for fraud, which of the following characteristics would make a revenue entry most suitable for selection?
choices: An automated entry generated by the billing system during the month
A manual entry posted by the CFO to revenue on the last day of the year with no supporting description
An entry that reverses a prior-month accrual in the normal course
A recurring entry for monthly subscription revenue with consistent amounts
exp: AU-C 240 points to entries made by individuals who do not usually make them, recorded at period end, to unusual accounts or with little explanation, as characteristic of fraudulent entries. Routine system-generated or recurring entries carry less risk of management override.

q: Under ASC 606, which condition must be met before a bill-and-hold arrangement supports revenue recognition while the client still holds the goods?
choices: The customer has paid at least half of the purchase price
The client has issued an invoice before year-end
The goods are insured by the customer
The reason for the arrangement is substantive and the product is identified as belonging to the customer and ready for physical transfer
exp: Bill-and-hold revenue requires a substantive reason (such as a customer request), separate identification of the product as the customer's, readiness for physical transfer, and that the client cannot use the product or direct it to another customer. Issuing an invoice or receiving partial payment does not transfer control.

q: An auditor confirms receivables as of October 31, two months before year-end, because controls are effective. What must the auditor do regarding the period from October 31 to December 31?
choices: Perform substantive procedures, or substantive procedures combined with tests of controls, covering the remaining period to provide a reasonable basis for extending conclusions to year-end
Nothing, because the confirmation date is within the fiscal year
Reconfirm every account as of December 31
Obtain management's written representation that no unusual transactions occurred
exp: When substantive procedures are performed at an interim date, AU-C 330 requires further procedures covering the remaining period, such as comparing balances and reviewing rollforward activity, so conclusions can be extended to period end. Reconfirming every account would defeat the purpose of interim testing, and a representation is not sufficient evidence.
